analysis.one_liner: Lets states and cities sue gun makers to recover the public costs of gun violence.
analysis.headline: The Gun Industry Responsibility Act, backed by 26 House members, died in the House Judiciary Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let state and local governments sue gun manufacturers to recover 'federal damages' — the money taxpayers spend on medical care for gunshot victims, law enforcement, and lost wages tied to gun violence. Governments that win would keep two-thirds of the money, earmarked for victims' compensation, police, schools, child care, and children's health care, and send one-third to Washington for crime prevention and firearm injury research. The idea was to give cities and states a financial incentive to sue the gun industry over unsafe design and oversupply of guns into illegal markets. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: State and local governments, which would gain a new legal tool and a funding stream for victims' compensation, law enforcement, schools, child care, and children's health care; taxpayers, who currently pick up most of the medical cost of firearm injuries; and communities affected by gun violence.

how_it_helps.text: States and cities could recover federal damages — medical expenses, continuing care, disability costs, law enforcement expenses, and lost wages — from gun manufacturers in lawsuits over the sale, distribution, use, or misuse of firearms [S2][S3].

Two-thirds of any money recovered stays with the state or local government, earmarked for gun-violence victims' compensation, injured and killed officers' families, law enforcement, and education, child care, and children's health care; one-third goes to the federal government for crime prevention and firearm injury research [S3].

The bill's findings note that at least 80 percent of the cost of treating firearm injuries is paid with taxpayer dollars, and that manufacturers generally did not include safety devices like child safety locks or loaded-chamber indicators [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearm manufacturers, distributors, and retailers, who would face new lawsuits and damage awards tied to the public costs of gun violence — costs that could be passed on to gun buyers through higher prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a new route to sue manufacturers of a lawful product for harm committed by third parties who misuse their products, a significant expansion of liability that gun makers and their supporters argued would hold an entire industry responsible for criminals' acts [S3].
Litigation on this scale would carry large legal costs, which the industry could pass along to lawful purchasers through higher prices [S3].

The bill gives the Attorney General the right to take over any such suit and bars states from recovering federal damages once the Justice Department files its own action, concentrating control over these claims in the federal executive branch [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill shifted real, measurable public costs — medical care, policing, victims' compensation — onto an industry whose products generate them, while funding services for victims and children. The honest counterweight is that it extended liability to manufacturers of a legal product for criminal misuse, with costs likely passed to buyers, and left the Justice Department with the power to preempt state suits. It was never tested in a hearing, so its design flaws were never examined or fixed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Harold Ford Jr. introduced the Gun Industry Responsibility Act in the House on March 11, 1999, with 14 original cosponsors [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed [S1][S5].
It gathered 25 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, but the committee never scheduled action before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers and sellers are better off because the bill died: they face no federal statutory route for governments to recover the public costs of gun violence, and no legal pressure to add safety devices or change distribution practices. Taxpayers and local governments continue to bear those costs.

for.name: Rep. Harold Ford Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 14 original cosponsors on the day of introduction

for.name: 25 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a full slate of supporters but no Republican backing

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; Chairman Henry Hyde (R-IL)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill in committee until the Congress ended

against.name: Gun industry and its advocacy allies
against.role: Firearms manufacturers and gun-rights lobbying groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation expanding gun-maker liability during this period, as cities began suing the industry over gun violence

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 25 cosponsors were Democrats; with Republicans in control of the House and its Judiciary Committee, the bill received no action.

industries.note: The bill would have let governments recover taxpayer costs of gun violence from the industry in court, creating financial pressure to add safety devices and curb oversupply into illegal markets. Its death left the industry free of that liability while the public continued paying those costs.
